name: Methylphenidate

lead: Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) is a prescription stimulant for ADHD and narcolepsy. Reduced appetite and weight loss are among its most common effects, so people who want to lean out discuss it as a way to eat less while staying focused.

The chain is lower appetite, fewer calories eaten, then fat loss. Its weight effects are documented as side effects in ADHD patients; it has not been tested as a weight-loss or cosmetic treatment in healthy people.

paras: It is prescribed as short- or extended-release tablets or capsules, usually taken in the morning. People who discuss it for leaning out pair it with calorie tracking and training. Appetite suppression is noticeable soon after dosing.

The US label carries a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction. Other documented effects include insomnia, anxiety, raised heart rate and blood pressure, rare psychiatric events and reduced growth in children. It is Schedule II in the US and Class B in the UK.

angle.text: Methylphenidate suppresses appetite, so people use it to eat less and get leaner, often alongside its focus effect. It is an ADHD stimulant; weight loss is a documented side effect and has not been tested as a goal.

lead: Methylphenidate, sold as Ritalin, Concerta and under many other brands, is a central nervous system stimulant prescribed mainly for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy [1][2]. It is a controlled substance in most countries, including Schedule II in the US and Class B in the UK [2].

Its relevance to appearance communities is as an appetite suppressant and, more distantly, as a drug with documented effects on body weight and growth. Loss of appetite and weight loss are among its most common side effects, and people who discuss stimulants as aids to eating less point to that effect [2][3]. Appetite suppression is temporary and tends to ease as each dose wears off, and severe weight loss is described as uncommon in treated ADHD patients [3]. Methylphenidate is not approved for weight control; amphetamine-class drugs such as amphetamine sulfate and methamphetamine carry that labelling instead [4].

The drug has been studied for more than seventy years. It was first synthesized in 1944, entered US medical use in the 1950s, and became one of the most prescribed ADHD medications worldwide [2]. Research covers ADHD symptoms, quality of life, cardiovascular and psychiatric safety, growth in children and cognitive effects in healthy adults [5][6][7]. No trial has tested methylphenidate as a weight-loss or cosmetic treatment in healthy people; its weight effects are documented as adverse effects in ADHD patients [2][8].
The US label carries a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction, and lists cardiovascular, psychiatric and blood-pressure precautions [1].
infobox: Ritalin, Concerta, Medikinet, Daytrana, Equasym, Biphentin and others [2]
About 2-3 hours; extended-release products act for 8-12 hours [2]
Schedule II (US); Class B (UK); Schedule III (Canada); Rx-only in EU [2]
Reduced appetite, weight loss, mild growth-rate reduction in children [2][3]

paras: Methylphenidate is a phenethylamine-class stimulant. It is dispensed as immediate-release tablets that act for roughly three to four hours, as extended-release capsules and tablets that act for eight to twelve hours, as a liquid, and as a skin patch [2]. Concerta, for example, releases about a fifth of its dose at once and the remainder over ten to twelve hours, whereas bedtime-dosed products such as Jornay PM delay release for hours [2].

Oral bioavailability is about 30 percent, peak blood levels occur around two hours after an immediate-release dose, the liver metabolizes most of it to ritalinic acid, and most of the dose is excreted in urine [2]. A meal raises absorption of immediate-release forms, and alcohol taken together can raise levels of the active d-isomer [2].

ADHD is the main approved indication, and the drug is first-line in children in most guidelines; narcolepsy is a second indication [2][8]. It is not approved for children under six in the US, although a 2022 Lancet Child and Adolescent Health trial tested methylphenidate with behavioural parent training in children aged three to five [2][9]. Off-label uses include treatment-resistant depression and apathy, with weak evidence [2]; a 2021 randomized trial (ADMET 2) examined apathy in Alzheimer disease [10]. The American Academy of Pediatrics guidance described in one reference summary recommends behavioural interventions first for ages four to five, with medication added if impairment persists, and medication plus behavioural therapy for older children [3].

Students sometimes use it as a study aid. A 2015 review summarized in Wikipedia found modest cognitive gains in healthy adults at therapeutic doses, while a reference summary notes no evidence that it improves grades in people without ADHD [2]. NIDA describes the broader pattern in which rising stimulant prescriptions over two decades have been accompanied by diversion and nonmedical use for cognitive enhancement among students and professionals [11]. Appetite suppression for weight control is not an approved or tested use of methylphenidate.

Appetite suppression and weight loss are among the most commonly reported side effects, and a 2024 systematic review found appetite suppression in children and adolescents [2]. The US label notes that adverse reactions such as weight loss occurred more often in the youngest children [1]. A reference summary of ADHD management says weight loss generally accompanies the reduced appetite, that the appetite effect is temporary and tends to return as the daily effect wears off, and that severe weight loss is very uncommon; nausea, dizziness and headache can also indirectly reduce eating [3].

Stimulants have a long history as diet aids. Amphetamine was sold as an appetite suppressant until restrictions in most countries from the late 1950s, and some amphetamine-class products still carry obesity labelling in the US, whereas methylphenidate is listed among compounds with known appetite-suppressant activity rather than as an approved weight treatment [4]. NIDA notes that stimulants were historically used to treat obesity and that this use has declined [11].

Researchers also report the opposite pattern over longer periods. A consensus statement cited by Wikipedia holds that long-term treatment removes the increased obesity risk associated with ADHD [2], and a 2026 JAMA Network Open study titled 'ADHD and Methylphenidate Use in Prepubertal Children and Adult BMI and Height' drew comment on Hacker News, where a commenter summarised its finding as higher adult BMI and slightly shorter height in adults with ADHD, especially those treated with methylphenidate; other commenters raised selection bias as an explanation [12]. These weight effects are therefore documented in patients rather than as a deliberate cosmetic outcome.

Long-term treatment in children is associated with a mild reduction in height [2]. Wikipedia gives an estimated effect of about 1 cm or less per year over the first three years of treatment, totalling roughly 3 cm across ten years [2]. A reference summary of ADHD management states that growth reductions are associated with prolonged stimulant treatment but that no causal relationship has been established and that the reductions do not appear to persist long-term [3].

Common adverse effects include dry mouth, anxiety, nausea, insomnia, abdominal pain, bruxism and small increases in blood pressure and heart rate; rare effects include worsening psychosis and priapism [2]. The label's boxed warning states that misuse can lead to addiction, overdose and death, with higher risk at higher doses or when the drug is snorted or injected [1]. It advises avoiding use in patients with serious structural cardiac disease and is contraindicated with monoamine oxidase inhibitors [1]. A reference summary rates abuse liability as moderate and similar to amphetamine, with dependence mainly reported in high-dose or nonmedical use [2].

Cardiovascular safety has been studied at scale. Wikipedia reports that 2011 FDA-commissioned studies found no association between medical use and serious cardiovascular events, and that a 2024 meta-analysis of 19 studies covering over 3.9 million participants found no significant association [2]. A 2009 FDA review of 49 trials, cited in a reference summary, found psychotic or manic symptoms in about 1.5 percent of children [3]. A 2025 JAMA Psychiatry systematic review quantified psychosis and bipolar disorder after stimulant exposure in people with ADHD [13]. A 2024 JAMA Network Open meta-analysis examined offspring outcomes after methylphenidate or atomoxetine in pregnancy [14]. A 2018 Cochrane review, described in Wikipedia, found a range of serious and nonserious adverse events in children but rated the quality of evidence from 260 studies as very low [2].

Routes matter. Snorting or injecting produces faster brain levels, greater euphoria and higher abuse potential than oral use, and injection of crushed tablets has caused abscesses and tissue necrosis [2]. NIDA lists dependence, withdrawal fatigue, sleep disruption, and with repeated misuse paranoia or psychosis among the risks of stimulant misuse, and notes that high doses can cause dangerously high body temperature and irregular heartbeat [11].

Methylphenidate blocks the dopamine and norepinephrine transporters, raising extracellular levels of both; unlike amphetamines it is not thought to cause monoamine release [2][15]. Wikipedia reports that in animal tissue it raises striatal and prefrontal dopamine and norepinephrine roughly three- to fourfold and that the d-threo isomer is the more active form [2]. The label states that its mode of therapeutic action in ADHD is not known [1]. Imaging studies with PET have used the drug to measure transporter occupancy [16].

Chemist Leandro Panizzon first synthesized methylphenidate in 1944 at Ciba, now part of Novartis. It was reported as a stimulant in 1954 and approved for medical use in the US in 1955, with Wikipedia also giving 1957 for its introduction [2]. The brand name Ritalin comes from Panizzon's wife Marguerite, nicknamed Rita, who reportedly used it for low blood pressure [2]. An early product, Centedrin, was a mixed-isomer preparation; later products contained only the threo form [2]. Early uses included reversing barbiturate coma, narcolepsy, depression and memory deficits in older people [2].

Use in children with hyperactivity grew from the 1960s, building on earlier work with Benzedrine, and production and prescriptions rose sharply from the 1990s, especially in the US [2]. Alza received FDA approval for extended-release Concerta in 2000 and the Daytrana patch was approved in 2006 [2]. Wikipedia lists methylphenidate as the 50th most prescribed US medication in 2023 with more than 13 million prescriptions [2]. Russia banned the drug for any use on 25 October 2014 [2]. In 2023 WHO guidelines recommended considering it for children aged six and older with ADHD, although it has not been added to the WHO Essential Medicines List [2].

Methylphenidate is Schedule II under the UN Convention on Psychotropic Substances and in the US, Schedule III in Canada, Class B in the UK (up to five years for possession without a prescription and up to fourteen for supply), Schedule 8 in Australia, and prescription-only in the EU [2]. Japan introduced regulations limiting access to prescribed methylphenidate in 2008 after illegal trade and medical complications from misuse rose [17]. The same 2015 review reports that around 4 percent of older teens and emerging adults in the US misuse methylphenidate each year [17].

Critics have objected to giving psychostimulants to children, and treatment has led to lawsuits over informed consent, side-effect information, misdiagnosis and coercive medication in schools [2]. The claim that childhood stimulant therapy leads to later drug abuse is described in Wikipedia as discredited by multiple sources, and people treated in childhood were less likely to have substance use disorders as adults [2]. Iceland has among the highest rates of use, and one study of 108 people who inject drugs found 88 percent had injected methylphenidate in the previous 30 days [2].

subs.h: Use in appearance and enhancement communities
paras: On forums, methylphenidate appears mostly in cognitive-enhancement and productivity discussions. A 2007 T Nation thread on 'brain function boosters' includes a poster comparing it with other stimulants, describing it as effective in the short term but noting preferences between immediate-release and time-released versions [18]. A 2021 Hacker News thread on a study of Ritalin and motivation shows the productivity framing [12]. Weight-loss framing is a smaller thread: people who discuss stimulants for eating less cite the appetite effect that ADHD patients report, a use that is neither approved nor studied for methylphenidate [2][3].

No studies have tested methylphenidate for weight loss or appearance goals in healthy people. Trials examine ADHD. A 2018 Lancet Psychiatry network meta-analysis compared amphetamines, atomoxetine, bupropion, clonidine, guanfacine, methylphenidate and modafinil across age groups for efficacy and tolerability at roughly 12, 26 and 52 weeks [5]. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 17 randomized trials with 5,388 participants found that amphetamines (Hedges g 0.51), methylphenidate (0.38) and atomoxetine (0.30) improved quality of life more than placebo in people with ADHD [6]. A 1971 study compared the subjective and physiological effects of amphetamine, methamphetamine, ephedrine, phenmetrazine and methylphenidate in people [19].

In healthy volunteers, a pilot randomized trial gave placebo, caffeine, methylphenidate or modafinil to men and tested cognition; methylphenidate improved self-reported fatigue and declarative memory 24 hours after learning, while all three stimulants were well tolerated [7]. Registered trials cover extended-release formulations in adults with ADHD [20], dermal reactions to a patch in 309 children [21], a Concerta-to-generic switch study in 1,464 participants [22] and use in epilepsy-related cognitive deficits [23].

lore.intro: Methylphenidate is discussed in enhancement and appetite-control corners of online communities, usually as a prescription stimulant that some people obtain outside medical care; forum material on it is thin and mostly concerns focus [18][12].
